topic.title: Time & Space Complexity
topic.summary: Big-O, Θ and Ω, how to count loops and recursion, and how to use input constraints to pick the right algorithm — the language every DSA answer is graded in.
topic.overview:
Every coding interview ends with **"What is the time and space complexity?"** — and a wrong or vague answer can sink an otherwise correct solution. Interviewers expect you to:

- state complexity **without being asked**, for both time and space, and say what n is;
- justify it by **counting** (loops, recursion tree, amortized argument), not by guessing from the code's shape;
- use the **input constraints** to know which complexity the intended solution has (n ≤ 10⁵ → O(n log n) or better);
- know the cost of every operation on the data structures you use (a hidden `includes` inside a loop is O(n²)).

**Core ideas**
1. Big-O is an upper bound on growth; drop constants and lower-order terms. Θ is tight, Ω is a lower bound.
2. Sequential code adds, nested code multiplies; halving gives log n; geometric series collapse to the largest term.
3. Recursion: work = number of nodes in the recursion tree; space = maximum depth.
4. Best / average / worst case is about the input; amortized is about a sequence of operations.

**How to study:** do the questions in order, then take the quiz. Afterwards, for every problem in the other DSA topics, write the complexity *before* reading the solution.

cheatsheet.title: Growth order
points: O(1) < O(log n) < O(√n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(n³) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)

cheatsheet.title: Constraints → target (≈10⁸ ops/s)
points: n ≤ 10⁸: O(n); larger: O(log n) / O(1)

cheatsheet.title: Counting rules
points: Sequential blocks add: O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²)
Different inputs keep different letters: O(n + m)

cheatsheet.title: Recursion
points: Space = max depth × frame size (fib: O(n))
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n); T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n)

cheatsheet.title: Data structure costs
points: Array: O(1) index, O(n) insert/delete in middle, O(1) amortized append
Hash map/set: O(1) average, O(n) worst
Heap: O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop, O(n) heapify

cheatsheet.title: Say it right
points: "O(n) time, O(1) extra space, where n is the array length"
Say "average" for hash maps and quicksort

patterns.name: Count the innermost statement
patterns.whenToUse: Any iterative code: write how many times the body runs for each outer iteration and sum the series.

template.code:
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)          // n times
  for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++)    // n-1-i times
    work();                          // total n(n-1)/2 -> O(n²)

patterns.name: Recursion tree
patterns.whenToUse: Recursive code: time = total nodes × work per node; space = depth of the tree.

patterns.name: Constraints → complexity
patterns.whenToUse: Before coding: read the maximum n and pick the slowest complexity under ~10⁸ operations.

patterns.name: Amortized analysis
patterns.whenToUse: Operations that are usually cheap but occasionally expensive (dynamic array resize, hash map rehash, monotonic stack): bound the total over n operations.

questions.title: What is Big-O notation? How is it different from Θ and Ω?
hints: Big-O is about how the running time grows when the input gets large, not about seconds.
Count how many times the innermost statement runs as a function of n.
T(n) = n² + n + 2. Which term still matters when n = 10⁶?

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Big-O is how fast the code runs." No growth idea, no definition, treats O, Θ and Ω as the same thing, cannot explain why constants are dropped.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Defines Big-O as an asymptotic upper bound on growth (with the c·g(n) definition), contrasts Θ (tight) and Ω (lower), explains dropping constants/lower terms with numbers, and analyses the code to O(n²).

solution.summary: Big-O describes how an algorithm's running time (or memory) grows as the input size n grows. It is an upper bound: f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than g up to a constant factor, so we keep only the dominant term — this function does n² + n + c steps, which is O(n²).
solution.explanation:
**Big-O** answers: *if the input doubles, what happens to the work?* We count basic steps as a function of the input size **n** and ignore machine speed.

**Formal definition.** f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are constants **c > 0** and **n₀** such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for every n ≥ n₀. In words: past some size, f is never more than a constant multiple of g.

**The three notations**
- **O (Big-O)** — upper bound: grows *no faster than* g. 3n² + 5n is O(n²), and also (loosely) O(n³).
- **Ω (Big-Omega)** — lower bound: grows *at least as fast as* g. Every comparison sort is Ω(n log n) in the worst case.
- **Θ (Big-Theta)** — tight bound: both O(g) and Ω(g). 3n² + 5n is Θ(n²).

In interviews people say "O" but mean the **tightest** bound they can prove, so always give the tight one (say O(n²), not O(n³)).

**Why drop constants and lower-order terms?**
1. For large n the biggest term dominates: at n = 1,000, n² = 1,000,000 while n = 1,000 (0.1%).
2. Constant factors depend on the language, CPU and compiler, not on the algorithm.
3. So 5n² + 3n + 20 → drop lower terms → 5n² → drop the constant → **O(n²)**.

**Analysing the snippet**
- Lines before the loops: constant work, O(1).
- First loop: n iterations, O(n).
- Nested loops: n × n = n² checks, O(n²).
- Total T(n) = n² + n + c → **O(n²) time**. Extra space is O(1) (a few variables).

**Rules of thumb:** sequential blocks **add** (O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²)); nested loops **multiply**; different inputs keep different letters (O(n + m), not O(n)).
keyPoints: Big-O = upper bound on growth rate as n → ∞, independent of hardware
Ω = lower bound, Θ = tight bound (both O and Ω)
Drop constants and lower-order terms because the dominant term decides growth
Sequential code adds, nested loops multiply, different inputs get different variables
Always state the tightest bound and say what n is

visuals.title: Which term of T(n) = n² + n + 2 matters?
visuals.caption: Blue = row just computed. In the last step the n² column (green) is ~100% of the work, so the other terms are dropped.

steps.note: Count steps of `sumAndZeroPairs`: n² pair checks + n additions + a constant 2. Fill the table for growing n and watch which column matters.
n = 1: the constant and the single loop are as big as the nested loop. Small inputs say nothing about growth.
n = 10: the nested loop already does 100 of the 112 steps.
n = 100: n² is ~99% of all work. The single loop (100 steps) is noise.
n = 1,000: a million pair checks vs a thousand additions. Doubling n now roughly **quadruples** T(n).
n = 10⁴: 10⁸ checks, about a second of simple work. The n and constant columns are invisible next to it.
n = 10⁶: 10¹² checks, hours of work. The lower-order terms would not change that.
For large n, T(n) behaves like n²: drop the lower-order terms and constants and say **O(n²)** (and since it is also at least n², it is Θ(n²)).

frames.note: Start from an exact count of steps, e.g. T(n) = 5n² + 3n + 20.
Drop the lower-order terms: for large n, 3n + 20 is negligible next to 5n².

visuals.title: O vs Θ vs Ω
rows: Upper bound: grows no faster than g(n)
Tight bound: grows exactly like g(n)
Lower bound: grows at least as fast as g(n)
f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
c₁·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
What people say in interviews (give the tight one)
Precise statements in textbooks and papers
"Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons"

pitfalls: Saying Big-O means "worst case" and Ω means "best case" — the notations are bounds on a function; best/worst case is a separate choice of input
Writing O(2n) or O(n² + n) instead of simplifying to O(n) and O(n²)
Merging different inputs: two loops over arrays of size n and m are O(n + m), not O(n)
Giving a loose bound (O(n³)) when the tight one is O(n²)

followUps.question: Can an O(n²) algorithm be faster than an O(n log n) one?
followUps.answer: Yes, for small n. Constants and cache behaviour matter there — that is why library sorts switch to insertion sort (O(n²)) for tiny subarrays.

followUps.question: Is O(n) also O(n²)?
followUps.answer: Technically yes (Big-O is only an upper bound), but it is a useless answer; give the tightest bound, Θ(n).

questions.title: Rank the common complexity classes and pick one from the input constraints
questions.prompt:
Order these from fastest to slowest growth: **O(n²), O(1), O(n!), O(n log n), O(log n), O(2ⁿ), O(n), O(n³)**, and give an example of each.

Then: a problem says **1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵** with a 1-second time limit. Which complexities are acceptable, and how do you decide?
hints: Plug in n = 1,000 and compare the numbers.
Logarithms grow very slowly (log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20); exponentials and factorials explode.
Assume about 10⁸ simple operations per second and compute the operation count for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Lists the classes in roughly the right order but cannot connect them to input sizes or give examples.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Gives the ordering with a canonical example for each, uses the ~10⁸ ops/second rule to turn constraints into a target complexity, and explains why n ≤ 10⁵ rules out O(n²).

solution.summary: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(n³) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!). With roughly 10⁸ simple operations per second, n ≤ 10⁵ means O(n²) = 10¹⁰ is too slow, so I aim for O(n log n) or O(n).
solution.explanation:
**Ranking with examples**

| Class | Name | Example |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | constant | array index, hash map get (average) |
| O(log n) | logarithmic | binary search, balanced BST lookup |
| O(n) | linear | one pass, two pointers, counting with a map |
| O(n log n) | linearithmic | merge sort, heap sort, sorting + scan |
| O(n²) | quadratic | all pairs, bubble/insertion sort |
| O(n³) | cubic | all triples, naive matrix multiplication |
| O(2ⁿ) | exponential | all subsets, naive recursive Fibonacci |
| O(n!) | factorial | all permutations (brute-force travelling salesman) |

**The 10⁸ rule.** A typical online judge or CPU does on the order of **10⁸ simple operations per second** (a rough figure: C++ is faster, Python slower). Turn the constraint into a budget:

1. Read the maximum n from the constraints.
2. Compute the operation count for each candidate complexity.
3. Pick the slowest complexity that stays under ~10⁸ (that is usually the intended solution).

For **n ≤ 10⁵**: n² = 10¹⁰ ✗, n log n ≈ 1.7×10⁶ ✓, n ✓. So the interviewer expects sorting, a heap, binary search, or a hash-map/two-pointer pass.

**Quick table** (memorise it): n ≤ 10 → O(n!); n ≤ 20 → O(2ⁿ); n ≤ 500 → O(n³); n ≤ 10⁴ → O(n²); n ≤ 10⁶ → O(n log n); n ≤ 10⁸ → O(n); bigger → O(log n) or O(1).

It works in reverse too: if n ≤ 20, the problem is *hinting* at subsets/bitmasks; if n ≤ 10⁵, a nested loop over all pairs is the brute force you should improve.
keyPoints: Correct order: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!
One concrete example per class
~10⁸ simple operations per second as a budget
Use the constraints to infer the intended complexity (n ≤ 10⁵ → O(n log n))
Small n (≤ 20) hints at exponential search

visuals.title: Operations needed for each class (budget ≈ 10⁸ per second)
visuals.caption: Green ≤ 10⁸ (fits in ~1 s), yellow ≤ 10⁹ (borderline), red > 10⁹ (too slow).

steps.note: Rule of thumb: a judge or server does roughly **10⁸ simple operations per second**. Fill in how many operations each class needs for typical input sizes.
**O(1)** constant: reading `arr[0]` costs the same for 10 or 10⁶ elements. Hash map get/set (average) and array indexing live here.
**O(log n)** logarithmic: `countHalvings` needs only ~20 iterations for n = 10⁶ because n halves each time. Binary search, balanced BST operations.
**O(n)** linear: `total` touches each element once. 10⁶ elements → 10⁶ steps, easily fast enough.
**O(n log n)**: sorting. At n = 10⁶ that is ~2×10⁷ steps — the go-to target when n ≤ 10⁶.
**O(n²)** quadratic: `countPairs` checks every pair. 10⁸ steps at n = 10⁴ is about the limit; at 10⁵ it is 10¹⁰ — far too slow.
**O(n³)** cubic: every triple. Fine for n = 500 (~10⁸), hopeless at 10⁴.
**O(2ⁿ)** exponential: every subset. n = 20 gives ~10⁶ subsets, n = 500 has more subsets than atoms in the universe.
**O(n!)** factorial: every ordering. 10! ≈ 3.6×10⁶ is fine, 20! ≈ 2.4×10¹⁸ is not. Only for n ≤ ~10.
Read it backwards in an interview: find the column for your n, and the **green** rows are the complexities that fit in ~1 second. Yellow is borderline, red will time out.

visuals.title: Constraint → expected complexity → typical techniques
rows: Sorting, heaps, binary search, ordered maps
Single pass, two pointers, hash map, prefix sums
Binary search on the answer, fast exponentiation, math formula

pitfalls: Putting O(n log n) above O(n²) or O(2ⁿ) below O(n³) — plug in n = 1,000 to check
Ignoring constraints and coding an O(n²) solution for n = 10⁵
Treating 10⁸ ops/second as exact — it is an order-of-magnitude rule
Forgetting that O(2ⁿ · n) code (subsets with copying) is still only OK for n ≈ 20

followUps.question: Where does O(√n) fit?
followUps.answer: Between O(log n) and O(n): for example trial division up to √n to test whether n is prime.

followUps.question: Is O(n log n) much worse than O(n)?
followUps.answer: Not by much in practice: log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20, so it is a factor of ~20. That is why "sort first" is often an acceptable step.

questions.title: Analyse the complexity of nested and non-linear loops
hints: Do not multiply loop headers blindly — count how many times the body actually runs.
For A, write the inner count for i = 0, 1, 2, … and add them up.
For B, after k iterations i = 2ᵏ. For C, add n + n/2 + n/4 + … (a geometric series).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Two loops so O(n²), one loop so O(n), two loops in C so O(n log n)." Pattern-matching on the shape gets C wrong and cannot justify A.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Counts body executions: A is an arithmetic series n(n−1)/2 → O(n²); B doubles i so it runs ⌈log₂ n⌉ times → O(log n); C is a geometric series < 2n → O(n).

solution.summary: Count how many times the innermost statement runs. A runs (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n−1)/2 times → O(n²); B multiplies i by 2 so it runs log₂ n times → O(log n); C does n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n work → O(n).
solution.explanation:
**A — dependent nested loops.** The inner loop length depends on i:

| i | 0 | 1 | 2 | … | n−1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| inner runs | n−1 | n−2 | n−3 | … | 0 |

Sum = (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 0 = **n(n−1)/2** (arithmetic series). That is n²/2 − n/2 → drop the constant ½ and the lower term → **O(n²)**. "Half the pairs" is still quadratic: doubling n quadruples the work.

**B — multiplicative loop.** After k iterations i = 2ᵏ. The loop stops when 2ᵏ ≥ n, i.e. k = ⌈log₂ n⌉ → **O(log n)**. Same for i /= 2, i *= 3 (log₃ n) — the base of the log is a constant factor, so we just write log n.

**C — the trap.** It looks like "log n outer × n inner = O(n log n)", but the inner loop shrinks: n + n/2 + n/4 + … + 1. A geometric series with ratio ½ sums to **less than 2n** → **O(n)**. (Binary-search-like halving plus linear work per level is O(n) when the work also halves.)

**General method**
1. Find what the innermost statement depends on (i, j, size…).
2. Write the number of runs per outer iteration.
3. Sum it: constant per iteration → multiply; arithmetic series → n²; geometric series → dominated by the biggest term.
4. Keep separate variables for separate inputs (n and m).

Space: all three use O(1) extra space.
keyPoints: Count executions of the innermost statement, do not just count loops
i *= 2 or i /= 2 → O(log n); the log base does not matter
Geometric series n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n → O(n)

visuals.title: A: triangle(6) — which (i, j) pairs run the body?
visuals.caption: Each number is the value of ops after that execution. Blue = current row, green = all executions: about half of the n × n square.

steps.note: Each cell (i, j) is one execution of `ops++`. Rows are outer iterations, columns are inner iterations. Watch how many cells each row fills.
i = 0: j runs from 1 to 5, so the body runs **5** times. Total ops = 5.
i = 1: j runs from 2 to 5, so the body runs **4** times. Total ops = 9.
i = 2: j runs from 3 to 5, so the body runs **3** times. Total ops = 12.
i = 3: j runs from 4 to 5, so the body runs **2** times. Total ops = 14.
i = 4: j runs from 5 to 5, so the body runs **1** time. Total ops = 15.
i = 5: j would start at 6, which is not < n, so the inner loop runs **0** times. Each row is one shorter than the last.
5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 15 = n(n−1)/2 = 6·5/2. That is about **half of an n × n square**, and half of n² is still **O(n²)**.

visuals.title: B: doubling(100) — i grows exponentially, so the loop is short
visuals.caption: Each cell is the value of i on one iteration; there are only ⌈log₂ n⌉ of them.

steps.note: `doubling(100)`: the loop variable is **multiplied** by 2, not incremented. How many times can you double 1 before reaching 100?
Iteration 1: i = 1 < 100, body runs. Then i becomes 2.
Iteration 2: i = 2 (= 2¹) < 100, body runs. Then i becomes 4.
Iteration 3: i = 4 (= 2²) < 100, body runs. Then i becomes 8.
Iteration 4: i = 8 (= 2³) < 100, body runs. Then i becomes 16.
Iteration 5: i = 16 (= 2⁴) < 100, body runs. Then i becomes 32.
Iteration 6: i = 32 (= 2⁵) < 100, body runs. Then i becomes 64.
Iteration 7: i = 64 (= 2⁶) < 100, body runs. Then i becomes 128.
i = 128 is not < 100, so the loop stops after **7** iterations = ⌈log₂ 100⌉. Doubling n adds just one more iteration: **O(log n)**.

visuals.title: Loop shapes you will meet, and their cost
rows: for i < n { for j < n }
for i < n { for j = i + 1; j < n }
for i < n { for (j = 1; j < n; j *= 2) }
for (s = n; s > 0; s = ⌊s / 2⌋) { for j < s }
for i < n { … } then for j < m { … }
for i < n { for j < m }

pitfalls: Answering O(n log n) for C because there are two loops and one halves
Writing O(n²/2) — constants are dropped, it is O(n²)
Using n for two different inputs: loops over arrays of size n and m are O(n·m) or O(n + m)
Forgetting hidden loops inside library calls (includes, indexOf, slice, splice are O(n))

followUps.question: What is the complexity of for (i = 0; i < n; i++) { arr.includes(x) } over an array of size n?
followUps.answer: O(n²): includes is itself a linear scan, so the loop body is O(n), not O(1).

followUps.question: What about for (i = 2; i < n; i = i * i)?
followUps.answer: i goes 2, 4, 16, 256, … (the exponent doubles), so it runs about log₂(log₂ n) times: O(log log n).

questions.title: Why is binary search O(log n)?
questions.prompt: Explain **why** binary search on a sorted array of n elements runs in **O(log n)** time. How many comparisons does it need, at most, for n = 1,000,000? What is its space complexity?
hints: What fraction of the remaining candidates does one comparison eliminate?
After k comparisons, how many candidates are left?
Solve n / 2ᵏ = 1 for k.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Because it splits the array in half." Correct intuition but no counting, no recurrence, and no number for n = 10⁶.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Shows the search space goes n → n/2 → n/4 → … → 1, solves n/2ᵏ = 1 to get k = log₂ n, writes T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), gives ~20 comparisons for 10⁶, and distinguishes iterative O(1) space from recursive O(log n).

solution.summary: Each comparison with the middle element discards half of the remaining candidates, so after k steps n/2ᵏ remain; the search ends when that reaches 1, i.e. after about log₂ n steps. For a million elements that is at most 20 comparisons.
solution.explanation:
**Counting the halvings**
1. Start with n candidates in [lo, hi].
2. Compare with arr[mid]. Because the array is **sorted**, one comparison tells us which half cannot contain the target, so we drop it.
3. Candidates: n → n/2 → n/4 → … → n/2ᵏ.
4. We stop when n/2ᵏ ≤ 1 ⇒ 2ᵏ ≥ n ⇒ **k = log₂ n** (precisely ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons in the worst case).

**As a recurrence:** T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1). Unrolling: T(n) = T(n/4) + 2 = T(n/8) + 3 = … = T(1) + log₂ n → **O(log n)**.

**Numbers that impress:** n = 10⁶ → 20 comparisons; n = 10⁹ → 30; every person on Earth (8×10⁹) → 33. A linear scan needs up to n.

**Space:** the iterative version keeps three integers → **O(1)**. A recursive version keeps one stack frame per halving → **O(log n)**.

**Why the array must be sorted:** sorting is what lets one comparison rule out half the elements. On unsorted data you can rule out only the one element you looked at, which is linear search. Sorting first costs O(n log n), so it only pays off if you search many times.

**Detail worth mentioning:** compute `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2` to avoid integer overflow in Java/C++ when lo + hi exceeds 2³¹ − 1.

complexity.time: O(log n) — the search space halves every iteration
complexity.space: O(1) iterative, O(log n) if written recursively

keyPoints: Each comparison halves the search space: n → n/2 → … → 1
n / 2ᵏ = 1 ⇒ k = log₂ n
Recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)
Concrete numbers: 10⁶ → 20 comparisons, 10⁹ → 30
Requires sorted (monotonic) data; iterative space O(1)

visuals.title: Searching for 77: the candidates shrink 10 → 5 → 2 → 1
visuals.caption: Red = half discarded by this comparison, grey = discarded earlier. The list on the right is the remaining search space.

steps.note: Search for 77 in 10 sorted numbers. The answer can be anywhere in [lo, hi] = [0, 9].
Iteration 1: mid = 4, arr[mid] = 27 < 77, so everything at or left of mid is too small. lo = 5. One comparison removed 5 of 10 candidates: 5 left.
Iteration 2: mid = 7, arr[mid] = 56 < 77, so everything at or left of mid is too small. lo = 8. One comparison removed 3 of 5 candidates: 2 left.
Iteration 3: mid = 8, arr[mid] = 63 < 77, so everything at or left of mid is too small. lo = 9. One comparison removed 1 of 2 candidates: 1 left.
Iteration 4: mid = 9, arr[mid] = 77 === 77. **Found** after 4 comparisons — a linear scan would need 10, and for n = 10⁶ binary search needs at most 20.

visuals.title: Unrolling the halving

frames.note: With 16 elements, every comparison halves what is left: 4 halvings leave 1 candidate, and one last comparison checks it — ⌊log₂ 16⌋ + 1 = 5 in the worst case.
frames.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  s0["16 candidates"] -->|"1 comparison"| s1["8"]
  s1 -->|"1 comparison"| s2["4"]
  s2 -->|"1 comparison"| s3["2"]
  s3 -->|"1 comparison"| s4["1"]
  s4 -->|"1 comparison"| s5["found / not found"]

frames.note: In general the size after k comparisons is n / 2ᵏ. Setting it to 1 gives k = log₂ n.
frames.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  a["n"] --> b["n / 2"]
  b --> c["n / 4"]
  c --> d["…"]
  d --> e["n / 2ᵏ = 1"]
  e --> f["k = log₂ n comparisons"]

visuals.title: Worst-case comparisons: linear vs binary search

pitfalls: Saying binary search works on any array — it needs sorted (or monotonic) data
Forgetting that sorting first costs O(n log n), which dominates a single search
Computing (lo + hi) / 2 in Java/C++ and overflowing for huge indices
Claiming a recursive version uses O(1) space

followUps.question: Is ternary search (split into 3) faster?
followUps.answer: No. It needs log₃ n iterations but 2 comparisons each, so 2·log₃ n ≈ 1.26·log₂ n comparisons — slightly more. Both are O(log n).

followUps.question: Can you binary search a linked list in O(log n)?
followUps.answer: No: reaching the middle node costs O(n) because there is no random access. That is why balanced BSTs or skip lists exist.

questions.title: What is the complexity of recursive Fibonacci, and how does memoization fix it?
hints: Draw the recursion tree for fib(5). How many nodes does it have?
Each call makes two calls, and the tree has depth n. What does that give?
With memoization, how many distinct values of n are ever computed?

approaches.name: Naive recursion
approaches.idea: Two calls per call, depth n: the recursion tree has up to 2ⁿ nodes. Stack depth is only n.

approaches.name: Memoization (top-down DP)
approaches.idea: Cache fib(k) the first time it is computed; later calls are O(1) lookups. n distinct subproblems, O(1) work each.

approaches.name: Bottom-up iteration
approaches.idea: Only the last two values are needed, so keep two variables in a loop.

solution.summary: The naive version branches into two calls at every level and the tree is n deep, so it does O(2ⁿ) work (tightly about 1.618ⁿ) because it recomputes the same subproblems; memoization computes each fib(k) once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space, and the bottom-up loop gets O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Recurrence for the naive version:** T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + O(1).
- Upper bound: T(n) ≤ 2·T(n−1) + O(1) ⇒ **O(2ⁿ)**.
- Tight bound: T(n) grows like fib(n) itself, Θ(φⁿ) with φ = (1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618. Saying O(2ⁿ) is accepted; mentioning φⁿ shows depth.
- The call count is exactly 2·fib(n+1) − 1: fib(5) makes 15 calls, fib(40) makes ~3.3×10⁸.

**Why so slow?** **Overlapping subproblems**: fib(5) computes fib(3) twice and fib(2) three times. The duplication compounds at every level.

**Space of the naive version is only O(n)**, not O(2ⁿ): the call stack holds one root-to-leaf path at a time, and the longest path has n frames. Time counts *all* nodes of the tree, space counts the *deepest* path.

**Memoization** stores each result the first time it is computed:
1. Base case n ≤ 1 → return n.
2. If memo has n → return it (O(1)).
3. Otherwise compute from n−1 and n−2, store, return.

Each n from 2..n is computed once and requested at most twice, so ~2n calls: **O(n) time**, O(n) memo + O(n) stack.

**Bottom-up** keeps only the last two values: **O(n) time, O(1) space**. (There is also an O(log n) method using matrix exponentiation — a good follow-up to mention.)

**General rule:** a recursion with **b** branches and depth **d** does up to **O(bᵈ)** work; memoization turns it into (number of distinct states) × (work per state).

complexity.time: Naive O(2ⁿ); memoized O(n); bottom-up O(n)
complexity.space: Naive O(n) stack; memoized O(n); bottom-up O(1)

keyPoints: Recursion tree: 2 branches per call, depth n → O(2ⁿ) (tight Θ(φⁿ))
Overlapping subproblems are recomputed
Space is the max stack depth O(n), not the number of calls
Memoization: distinct states × work per state = O(n)
Bottom-up keeps two variables → O(1) space

visuals.title: Recursion tree of the naive fib(5)
visuals.caption: Blue = calls at the current depth, light blue = base cases. Yellow/red = the same subproblem solved more than once.

steps.note: `fib(5)` is not a base case, so it calls `fib(4)` and `fib(3)`.
Level 1: 2 calls. Each non-base call again makes **two** calls — the tree doubles in width.
Level 2: 4 calls. Notice `fib(3)` appears a second time and `fib(2)` already twice: the same work is being redone.
Level 3: the base cases (`n <= 1`, light blue) stop the branching; the others keep splitting.
Level 4: the deepest path is fib(5) → fib(4) → fib(3) → fib(2) → fib(1): depth n, so the call stack never holds more than ~n frames.
Repeated work: `fib(3)` is computed 2 times and `fib(2)` 3 times. For bigger n the duplicates explode — fib(30) calls fib(2) over 500,000 times.
fib(5) = 5 took **15 calls** (2·fib(n+1) − 1). Each level can double, so the work is bounded by **O(2ⁿ)** (tightly Θ(φⁿ), φ ≈ 1.618).

visuals.title: fibMemo(5): the memo cuts off repeated subtrees
visuals.caption: Calls appear in execution order. Green = answered from the memo without recursing.

steps.note: fibMemo(5) is not in memo yet, so it recurses into fibMemo(4) first.
fibMemo(4) is not in memo yet, so it recurses into fibMemo(3) first.
fibMemo(3) is not in memo yet, so it recurses into fibMemo(2) first.
fibMemo(2) is not in memo yet, so it recurses into fibMemo(1) first.
fibMemo(1) is a base case: return 1.
fibMemo(0) is a base case: return 0.
fibMemo(2) finished and was stored in memo. fibMemo(1) is a base case: return 1.
fibMemo(3) finished and was stored in memo. fibMemo(2) is **already in memo** (= 1): return it immediately. The whole subtree that the naive version would rebuild is skipped.
fibMemo(4) finished and was stored in memo. fibMemo(3) is **already in memo** (= 2): return it immediately. The whole subtree that the naive version would rebuild is skipped.
Done: fibMemo(5) = 5 in **9 calls** instead of 15. Every n from 2 to 5 is computed once and later requests are O(1) memo hits (green), so time is **O(n)**; the memo and the stack are O(n) space.

visuals.title: How many calls? (time column assumes ~10⁸ calls per second)

pitfalls: Saying the naive version uses O(2ⁿ) space — only one path is on the stack at a time, so O(n)
Calling memoized Fibonacci O(1) — it is O(n) the first time
Creating a new memo inside every call (memo must be shared across the recursion)
Ignoring overflow: fib(93) exceeds a 64-bit signed long, and JS numbers lose precision after fib(78)

followUps.question: Can you compute fib(n) faster than O(n)?
followUps.answer: Yes: [[1,1],[1,0]]ⁿ gives fib(n) and fast matrix exponentiation needs O(log n) multiplications.

followUps.question: Memoization vs tabulation?
followUps.answer: Memoization is top-down recursion plus a cache (computes only needed states, uses stack). Tabulation fills a table bottom-up with loops (no recursion limit, often less space).

questions.title: What is space complexity, and why does recursion use memory?
hints: Space complexity counts memory that grows with n — not only arrays and maps.
Where does a function store its argument and "what to do after the call returns"?
How many unfinished calls of sumTo exist at the moment sumTo(0) runs?

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "sumTo uses no arrays, so it is O(1) space." Misses the call stack entirely and cannot explain the crash.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Defines auxiliary space, explains stack frames, shows recursion depth n → O(n) space and stack overflow (~10⁴ frames in Node, 1,000 in Python by default), contrasts with the O(1) loop, and notes output space.

solution.summary: Space complexity is how the extra memory an algorithm needs grows with the input. Recursion is not free: every pending call keeps a stack frame, so sumTo(n) has n + 1 frames alive at its deepest point — O(n) space and a stack overflow for large n — while the loop version uses O(1).
solution.explanation:
**What counts**
- **Auxiliary (extra) space**: memory the algorithm allocates beyond the input — variables, arrays, maps, *and the call stack*. This is what interviewers usually mean.
- **Total space** = input + auxiliary. Say which one you mean if it matters.
- The output is often excluded ("O(1) extra space besides the output array"), but say so explicitly — `prefixSums` needs O(n) for its result.

**The call stack.** Each function call pushes a **stack frame** with its parameters, local variables and return address. The frame is popped when the call returns. A recursive call that has not returned yet keeps its frame alive.

For `sumTo(n)`:
1. sumTo(n) waits for sumTo(n−1), which waits for sumTo(n−2), …
2. When sumTo(0) runs, **n + 1 frames** are on the stack.
3. Space is the **maximum depth**, so O(n).

**Stack overflow.** The stack is a small fixed-size region (V8 gives Node.js just under 1 MB by default). In Node.js a simple recursion like this fails after roughly 10,000 frames with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` (the exact number depends on frame size). Python stops at a default recursion limit of 1,000; Java throws `StackOverflowError` (stack size set by `-Xss`).

**Fixes:** rewrite as a loop (sumToIter, O(1)), use an explicit stack on the heap for DFS-style code, or reduce depth (recurse on the smaller half in quicksort → O(log n)). JavaScript engines in practice do not perform tail-call optimisation (only Safari does), so do not rely on it.

**Recursion space rule:** space = max depth × space per frame. Balanced divide-and-conquer (binary search, merge sort) → O(log n) depth; linear recursion (linked list, sumTo) → O(n); tree DFS → O(h).
keyPoints: Space complexity = extra memory as a function of n (say if you exclude the output)
Every unfinished call holds a stack frame; space = maximum recursion depth
sumTo is O(n) space, sumToIter is O(1) — same O(n) time
Deep recursion overflows: ~10⁴ frames in Node, 1,000 in Python by default
Convert to iteration or an explicit stack to avoid overflow

visuals.title: Call stack of sumTo(4)
visuals.caption: Top of the stack is the last item. The stack grows to n + 1 sumTo frames before anything returns.

steps.note: main() calls sumTo(4). Every call gets a **stack frame** holding its argument and where to continue after the callee returns.
sumTo(4) cannot finish until sumTo(3) returns, so its frame stays on the stack and a new frame is pushed.
sumTo(3) cannot finish until sumTo(2) returns, so its frame stays on the stack and a new frame is pushed.
sumTo(2) cannot finish until sumTo(1) returns, so its frame stays on the stack and a new frame is pushed.
sumTo(1) cannot finish until sumTo(0) returns, so its frame stays on the stack and a new frame is pushed.
sumTo(0) hits the base case. The stack is now at its **deepest**: n + 1 = 5 sumTo frames.
sumTo(0) returns 0 and its frame is **popped**. sumTo(1) can now compute 1 + 0.
sumTo(1) returns 1 and is popped. The stack unwinds one frame at a time.
sumTo(2) returns 3 and is popped. The stack unwinds one frame at a time.
sumTo(3) returns 6 and is popped. The stack unwinds one frame at a time.
sumTo(4) returns **10** to main(). Peak usage was 5 frames for n = 4: memory grows linearly with n, so the space complexity is **O(n)** even though no array was allocated.

visuals.title: Call stack of sumToIter(4) — constant space
visuals.caption: The loop updates variables inside one frame instead of pushing new frames.

steps.note: main() calls sumToIter(4): **one** frame holding n, total and i.
i = 1: total = 1. The loop reuses the same variables — nothing new is pushed.
i = 2: total = 3. Still the same single frame.
i = 3: total = 6. Still the same single frame.
i = 4: total = 10. Still the same single frame.
Return 10. Same O(n) time as the recursive version, but the stack never grew: **O(1)** extra space, and no stack-overflow risk for n = 10⁶.

visuals.title: Where the extra space comes from
rows: n + 1 frames at the deepest point
Recursive version keeps one frame per halving
Hash map / memo of n items
Temporary arrays when merging (+ O(log n) stack)
Recursion depth depends on the pivots
DFS on a tree of height h
O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed
The queue holds a whole level (w = max width, up to ~n/2)

pitfalls: Forgetting the call stack when stating space for recursive code
Saying recursion depth equals the number of calls (fib makes O(2ⁿ) calls but is only n deep)
Not saying whether the output array is counted
Relying on tail-call optimisation in JavaScript or Java (neither guarantees it in practice)

followUps.question: How do you make a recursive DFS safe for a 10⁶-node path graph?
followUps.answer: Use an explicit stack (array) in a loop. Heap memory is much larger than the call stack, so depth is no longer limited by frames.

followUps.question: What is the space complexity of in-place quicksort?
followUps.answer: O(log n) average for the recursion stack, O(n) worst case. Recursing into the smaller partition first and looping on the larger keeps it O(log n) even in the worst case.

questions.title: Why is appending to a dynamic array O(1) amortized?
questions.prompt: JavaScript arrays, Java's `ArrayList` and Python's `list` are backed by a fixed-size buffer. When it is full, a bigger buffer is allocated and every element is copied — an O(n) operation. Why do we still say **push / add / append is O(1)**? What would go wrong if the buffer grew by a constant amount instead of doubling?
hints: How often does a resize happen if the capacity doubles each time?
Add up the copies for n pushes: 1 + 2 + 4 + … up to n.
Amortized cost = total cost of n operations ÷ n.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Push is O(1) because you just write at the end." Ignores resizing, or says "sometimes O(n)" without explaining why the average is still O(1).

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains capacity vs length, shows that with doubling the copies form a geometric series < 2n, so n pushes cost O(n) total → O(1) amortized; contrasts with +k growth (O(n²) total) and distinguishes amortized from average-case.

solution.summary: Most pushes write into a spare slot in O(1). When the buffer is full it doubles, copying n elements — but that happens only at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, …, so all copies over n pushes add up to less than 2n. Total work for n pushes is O(n), which is O(1) per push on average over the sequence: amortized O(1).
solution.explanation:
**Two numbers:** *length* (elements stored) and *capacity* (size of the underlying buffer).
- If length < capacity, push writes one slot: **O(1)**.
- If length == capacity, allocate a buffer of 2 × capacity, copy all elements (**O(n)**), then write.

**Aggregate analysis (the 30-second proof).** Starting at capacity 1, resizes copy 1, 2, 4, …, 2ᵏ elements where 2ᵏ < n. Geometric sum: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 < 2n. Plus n writes. **Total < 3n = O(n)** for n pushes ⇒ **O(1) amortized** per push.

**Banker's (accounting) view.** Charge every push 3 coins: 1 pays for its own write, 2 are saved. When the buffer of size m fills, the m/2 elements pushed since the last resize have saved m coins — exactly enough to copy all m elements.

**Why the growth must be multiplicative.** Grow by a constant k instead: a resize happens every k pushes and copies the whole array, so total copies ≈ k + 2k + 3k + … ≈ n²/(2k) → **O(n) amortized per push**. Any factor > 1 works (Java's ArrayList grows by 1.5×); bigger factors mean fewer copies but more wasted space.

**Amortized ≠ average case.** Amortized is a *guarantee* over any sequence of operations (no randomness). Average case assumes a distribution of inputs. A single push can still take O(n) — matters for real-time systems (a game frame, a trading system), which is why some systems pre-size: `new ArrayList<>(n)`, or reserve capacity.

**Shrinking:** halve the buffer when it is **¼** full, not ½ — otherwise alternating push/pop at the boundary would resize every time (thrashing).
keyPoints: Capacity vs length; resize copies everything
Doubling: copies 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n, so n pushes cost O(n)
Amortized O(1) is a worst-case guarantee over a sequence, not an average over inputs
Constant-increment growth gives O(n²) total — growth must be geometric
A single push can still be O(n); pre-size when you know n

visuals.title: Pushing A…H into a doubling array
visuals.caption: Yellow = elements copied during a resize, blue = the newly written element, · = an allocated but unused slot.

steps.note: Start with capacity 1 and nothing stored. The **capacity** is the size of the real fixed-size buffer; **length** is how many slots are used.
push(A): length 0 < capacity 1, so just write it at index 0. Cost 1. The buffer is now full: the next push must resize.
push(B): length 1 === capacity 1, so the buffer is full. Allocate capacity 2, **copy 1** element, then write B. This push costs 2.
push(C): length 2 === capacity 2, so the buffer is full. Allocate capacity 4, **copy 2** elements, then write C. This push costs 3.
push(D): length 3 < capacity 4, so just write it at index 3. Cost 1. The buffer is now full: the next push must resize.
push(E): length 4 === capacity 4, so the buffer is full. Allocate capacity 8, **copy 4** elements, then write E. This push costs 5.
push(F): length 5 < capacity 8, so just write it at index 5. Cost 1. 2 spare slots left for more cheap pushes.
push(G): length 6 < capacity 8, so just write it at index 6. Cost 1. 1 spare slot left for more cheap pushes.
push(H): length 7 < capacity 8, so just write it at index 7. Cost 1. The buffer is exactly full now.

8 pushes cost 8 writes + 7 copies = 15. The copies 1 + 2 + 4 + … always add up to less than 2n (here 7 < 16), so n pushes cost less than 3n in total: the **amortized** cost per push is O(1) even though a single push can be O(n).

visuals.title: Cost of each push laid end to end
visuals.caption: One unit = one element written or copied. Copies cluster at pushes 2, 3 and 5; everything else costs 1.

steps.note: push A: capacity 1 has a free slot, one write. Cost 1.
push B: capacity 1 is full, so copy 1 element into a buffer of 2, then write. Cost 2. The new buffer is full again right away.
push C: capacity 2 is full, so copy 2 elements into a buffer of 4, then write. Cost 3. That resize buys 1 cheap push next.
push E: capacity 4 is full, so copy 4 elements into a buffer of 8, then write. Cost 5. That resize buys 3 cheap pushes next.
push H: one write. Since the last resize, pushes cost 1 each: they are using the spare slots that resize created.
Total work 15 units for 8 pushes (≈1.9 per push). Spread each big copy over the cheap pushes that follow it and the average stays below 3 units per push for any n: **O(1) amortized**.

visuals.title: Growth strategy decides the amortized cost
rows: Classic textbook choice; at most half the buffer unused
Java's ArrayList (old + old/2): less wasted memory, a few more copies
Resizes every k pushes and copies everything each time
Every push copies the whole array
Shrink to ½ when ¼ full
Shrinking at ½ full would thrash on push/pop at the boundary

pitfalls: Saying every push is O(1) — a single push can be O(n); only the amortized cost is O(1)
Confusing amortized cost with average-case cost over random inputs
Growing by a constant amount (O(n²) total) in a hand-written dynamic array
Shrinking at half full, which causes resize thrashing

followUps.question: Is unshift / insert at index 0 also amortized O(1)?
followUps.answer: No. It shifts every element one slot right on every call: O(n) each time. Use a deque (circular buffer) for O(1) at both ends.

followUps.question: Where else does amortized analysis appear?
followUps.answer: Hash map resizing (rehash all keys when the load factor is exceeded), the two-stack queue, union-find with path compression, and monotonic stacks (each element is pushed and popped once).

questions.title: Time complexity of operations on common data structures
questions.prompt:
Give the time complexity of **access, search, insert and delete** for: array (dynamic array), linked list, hash map, balanced BST, binary heap, and stack/queue. For each, say when you would choose it.

Bonus: which of these JavaScript array methods are O(n)? `push, pop, shift, unshift, includes, splice`
hints: Arrays give O(1) access by index because the address is computed directly.
Inserting into the middle of an array means moving everything after it.
Hash maps trade order for O(1) average lookup; BSTs keep order at O(log n); heaps only give fast access to the min (or max).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Recites "hash map O(1), array O(n)" without saying which operation, ignores average vs worst case, and cannot say when to use a heap or BST.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Gives per-operation costs with average vs worst case and amortized notes, explains *why* (address arithmetic, shifting, hashing, tree height), and maps each structure to the problems it is best for.

solution.summary: Array: O(1) index access, O(n) search and middle insert/delete, O(1) amortized append. Linked list: O(n) access, O(1) insert/delete at a known node. Hash map: O(1) average insert/lookup/delete, O(n) worst. Balanced BST: O(log n) for everything plus sorted order. Heap: O(1) peek min, O(log n) push/pop. Stack/queue: O(1) at the ends.
solution.explanation:
**Why each cost is what it is**
- **Array**: elements are contiguous, so `address = base + i × size` → O(1) access. Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts the tail → O(n). Append is O(1) amortized (doubling). Unsorted search is O(n); a **sorted** array allows binary search in O(log n).
- **Linked list**: no address arithmetic, so reaching index i walks i nodes → O(n). Once you hold a node (and its predecessor), insert/delete is just pointer rewiring → O(1). Doubly linked lists power LRU caches.
- **Hash map / set**: hash the key → bucket index → O(1) **average**. Worst case O(n) if many keys collide (Java 8+ turns long chains into red-black trees, which improves that to O(log n) for Comparable keys). No ordering.
- **Balanced BST** (Java `TreeMap`, C++ `std::map`): height stays O(log n), so search/insert/delete are O(log n), plus in-order traversal, min/max, floor/ceiling and range queries. An **unbalanced** BST can degrade to a linked list: O(n).
- **Binary heap** (`PriorityQueue`, Python `heapq`): peek min/max O(1), push/pop O(log n) (sift up/down the height), build from n items O(n), search for an arbitrary value O(n).
- **Stack / queue**: push/pop or enqueue/dequeue at the ends in O(1). Use `ArrayDeque` in Java, `collections.deque` in Python; in JS avoid `shift()` in a hot loop — treat it as O(n), and use a head index instead.

**JavaScript array methods:** push/pop O(1); shift, unshift, splice, includes, indexOf O(n); sort O(n log n). A loop calling `includes` is a hidden O(n²) — use a `Set`.

**How to pick:** lookup by key → hash map; sorted order / ranges → balanced BST; repeated min/max → heap; LIFO/FIFO → stack/queue; index access and iteration → array.

code.code:
const arr = [5, 1, 4];
arr.push(9);               // O(1) amortized: write at the end
arr.pop();                 // O(1)
arr[1];                    // O(1): index -> address arithmetic
arr.includes(4);           // O(n): linear scan
arr.unshift(0);            // O(n): shifts every element right
arr.shift();               // O(n): shifts every element left
arr.splice(1, 1);          // O(n): shifts the tail
arr.sort((a, b) => a - b); // O(n log n)

const scores = new Map();
scores.set('alice', 90);   // O(1) average
scores.get('alice');       // O(1) average
scores.has('bob');         // O(1) average
scores.delete('alice');    // O(1) average

const seen = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
seen.has(2);               // O(1) average (arr.includes(2) would be O(n))

keyPoints: Array: O(1) access, O(n) middle insert/delete, O(1) amortized append
Hash map: O(1) average, O(n) worst; no order
Balanced BST: O(log n) with ordering and range queries
Heap: O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop, O(n) build
Know your language: shift/unshift/includes/splice are O(n) in JS

visuals.title: Operation costs at a glance
visuals.caption: * amortized. Hash map costs are average case; worst case is O(n) when keys collide.
rows: O(1)* at end, O(n) in middle
O(1) at end, O(n) in middle

visuals.title: Which data structure do I need?

frames.note: First question: do you look things up by key or ask "have I seen this?" — that is a hash map or set.
Ordering needs a tree: a balanced BST keeps keys sorted with O(log n) operations.
Repeated min/max is the job of a heap; otherwise the access order decides between stack, queue and plain array.

pitfalls: Quoting hash map O(1) without "average" — the worst case is O(n)
Saying linked-list insert is O(1) without noting that finding the position is O(n)
Using arr.shift() as a queue or arr.includes() inside a loop (hidden O(n))
Forgetting that an unbalanced BST can degrade to O(n)

followUps.question: Why are arrays often faster than linked lists even for O(n) work?
followUps.answer: Contiguous memory is cache-friendly: the CPU loads neighbouring elements together. Linked-list nodes are scattered, so each step can be a cache miss.

followUps.question: How do you find the k-th smallest element quickly?
followUps.answer: A heap gives O(n + k log n) or O(n log k); quickselect gives O(n) average; a BST augmented with subtree sizes gives O(log n) per query.

questions.title: Best, average and worst case — what is the difference?
hints: For linear search: where is the target when the search is fastest? Slowest?
For quicksort: what happens when the pivot is always the largest element?
Big-O / Ω / Θ are bounds on a function; best/worst/average describe which input you analyse. They are independent choices.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Best case is Ω, average is Θ, worst is O." A very common mix-up; also no concrete input that triggers each case.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Defines each case by the input, gives linear search (1 / n/2 / n) and quicksort (n log n / n log n / n² on sorted input with a last-element pivot), explains randomized pivots, and separates case analysis from O/Θ/Ω.

solution.summary: The case describes which input of size n we analyse: best = the luckiest input, worst = the unluckiest, average = the expected cost over a distribution of inputs. Linear search is O(1) best and O(n) average and worst; this quicksort is O(n log n) best/average but O(n²) worst on already-sorted input, which random or median-of-three pivots avoid.
solution.explanation:
**Definitions** (for a fixed input size n)
- **Best case**: the minimum work over all inputs of size n.
- **Worst case**: the maximum work. This is the default in interviews because it is a guarantee.
- **Average case**: expected work under an assumed input distribution (e.g. "target equally likely at any position", "all permutations equally likely").

**Linear search**
- Best: target at index 0 → 1 comparison → O(1).
- Worst: target last or missing → n comparisons → O(n).
- Average (target present, uniform position): (n + 1)/2 comparisons → still **O(n)**.

**Quicksort with a last-element pivot**
- Each level of recursion partitions in O(n) total.
- **Good pivots** (near the median) halve the problem → log₂ n levels → **O(n log n)** best and average.
- **Bad pivots**: on an **already sorted** array the last element is always the maximum, so one side is empty: n levels, (n−1) + (n−2) + … = n(n−1)/2 comparisons → **O(n²)**. Reverse-sorted input and arrays where every value is equal are just as bad with this partition (the pivot keeps ending up at one end). Sorted input is common in real data, so this matters.
- Fixes: pick a **random pivot** (expected O(n log n) for *every* input with distinct values; many duplicates also need a three-way partition), **median-of-three**, or switch to heapsort when recursion gets too deep (introsort, used by C++ `std::sort`). Java sorts primitives with dual-pivot quicksort and objects with TimSort.

**Case ≠ notation.** O, Ω and Θ are bounds on a function; best/average/worst choose *which* function. You can say "the worst case of quicksort is Θ(n²)" and "the best case is Θ(n log n)". Saying "Ω means best case" is a classic mistake.

**Amortized** is different again: the worst-case total over a *sequence* of operations, divided by the number of operations (dynamic array push).
keyPoints: Cases are about the input; O/Ω/Θ are about bounds — they are independent
Linear search: O(1) best, O(n) average and worst
Quicksort: O(n log n) best/average, O(n²) worst on sorted input with a first/last pivot
Random pivot or median-of-three makes the bad case very unlikely
Interviews default to worst case; say "average" explicitly for hash maps and quicksort

visuals.title: Quicksort recursion on sorted input — worst case
visuals.caption: Each node is one call, labelled with its subarray size. Blue = current depth.

steps.note: Sorted input [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]: the pivot (last element) 7 is the **largest**, so partition leaves 6 elements on the left and 0 on the right.
Depth 1: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] pivot 6. This level does 5 comparisons.
Depth 2: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] pivot 5. This level does 4 comparisons.
Depth 3: [1, 2, 3, 4] pivot 4. This level does 3 comparisons.
Depth 4: [1, 2, 3] pivot 3. This level does 2 comparisons.
Depth 5: [1, 2] pivot 2. This level does 1 comparison.
Depth 6: [1] (size 1, returns). This level does 0 comparisons.
Sorted input is the **worst case**: every pivot is the maximum, so each call peels off just one element. 7 levels, 21 = n(n−1)/2 comparisons → **O(n²)**.

visuals.title: Quicksort recursion with balanced pivots — best/average case
visuals.caption: Same 7 numbers in a different order: the pivot lands in the middle every time.

steps.note: Input [3, 1, 2, 6, 5, 7, 4]: the last element 4 is the **median**, so partition splits the 7 elements 3 | 3.
Depth 1: [3, 1, 2] pivot 2; [5, 7, 6] pivot 6. This level does 4 comparisons.
Depth 2: [1] (size 1, returns); [3] (size 1, returns); [5] (size 1, returns); [7] (size 1, returns). This level does 0 comparisons.
Balanced splits: 3 levels × at most n comparisons each = 10 comparisons. In general log₂ n levels × O(n) per level → **O(n log n)**, the best and average case.

pitfalls: Equating Ω with best case and O with worst case
Quoting quicksort as O(n log n) without "average" — the worst case is O(n²)
Calling the average case "the case for random input" without stating the assumption
Confusing amortized cost with average-case cost

followUps.question: Why is quicksort often faster than merge sort in practice despite its O(n²) worst case?
followUps.answer: It sorts in place with sequential memory access (cache-friendly) and small constants; with a random pivot the O(n²) case is astronomically unlikely.

followUps.question: How can an attacker exploit worst cases?
followUps.answer: By crafting inputs: sorted data against a naive quicksort, or many colliding keys against a hash table (HashDoS). Randomized pivots and seeded hashing defend against this.

quiz.question: Simplify O(4n² + 100n + 7000).
quiz.explanation: Drop lower-order terms (100n + 7000) and the constant factor 4. O(4n²) describes the same growth but is not simplified.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of this function (tightest Big-O bound)?
quiz.explanation: The inner loop runs n, n−1, …, 1 times: n(n+1)/2 in total, which is O(n²) (O(n²/2) is the same class — constants are dropped). O(n³) is a true but loose upper bound, not the tight answer.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of this loop (tightest Big-O bound)?
quiz.explanation: After k iterations i = 3ᵏ, so the loop runs about log₃ n times. The base of the logarithm is a constant factor, so it is O(log n). O(n/3) would be a loop with i += 3.

quiz.question: A problem has n ≤ 2 × 10⁵ and a 1-second limit. Which is the slowest complexity you can safely aim for?
quiz.explanation: n log n ≈ 3.5 × 10⁶ operations, well under ~10⁸. O(n²) would be 4 × 10¹⁰, roughly minutes — too slow.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of the naive recursive Fibonacci fib(n) = fib(n−1) + fib(n−2)?
quiz.explanation: Each call branches into two and the tree is n deep, so the number of calls is bounded by 2ⁿ (tightly Θ(φⁿ), φ ≈ 1.618). O(n) is the memoized version.

quiz.question: What is the extra space complexity of this function (tightest Big-O bound)?
quiz.explanation: No arrays are allocated, but n + 1 calls are on the call stack at the deepest point, each with its own frame. That is O(n) space (and a stack overflow for very large n).

quiz.question: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. What is the amortized cost of one push?
quiz.explanation: Resizes copy 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n elements over n pushes, so the total is O(n) and the cost per push is O(1) amortized — even though a single resizing push is O(n).

quiz.question: Which statement about Θ (Big-Theta) is correct?
options: f = Θ(g) means f grows no faster than g
f = Θ(g) means f = O(g) and f = Ω(g)
Θ describes the average case, O the worst case
Θ can only be used for recursive algorithms
quiz.explanation: Θ is a tight bound: both an upper bound (O) and a lower bound (Ω). Bounds and cases are independent — "grows no faster than" is the definition of O alone.

quiz.question: Quicksort that always picks the last element as pivot is run on an already sorted array of n elements. What is its running time?
quiz.explanation: The pivot is always the maximum, so each partition removes only one element: (n−1) + (n−2) + … = O(n²). A random pivot makes the expected time O(n log n) for any input with distinct values.

quiz.question: a has length n and b has length m. What is the time complexity (tightest Big-O bound)?

code.code:
for (const x of a) console.log(x);
for (const y of b) console.log(y);

quiz.explanation: The loops run one after the other, so their costs add: O(n + m). They would multiply only if one were nested inside the other. Writing O(n) ignores that b can be much larger.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time of a lookup in a hash map that resolves collisions with plain linked-list chaining?
quiz.explanation: If every key hashes to the same bucket, a lookup scans a chain of n entries: O(n). O(1) is only the average case. (Java 8+ converts long chains into balanced trees, improving that to O(log n) when the keys are Comparable.)

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of this function (tightest Big-O bound)?
quiz.explanation: The inner loop runs n + n/2 + n/4 + … + 1 < 2n times — a geometric series. The outer loop runs log n times, but the inner work shrinks, so the total is O(n), not O(n log n).
